Twelve ships sailed into a harbor in Sicily. Almost everyone on board was dead.
It was October 1347, and the port was Messina.
The few sailors still alive had black swellings the size of an egg.
The city ordered the ships back out to sea. It was already too late.
Rats and fleas had come ashore, carrying a bacterium called Yersinia pestis.
Within four years, it killed up to half the people in Europe.
It became the deadliest pandemic in recorded history.
